reason: This passage from 1 Samuel 19-20 depicts King Saul consumed with personal jealousy and paranoia regarding David's growing popularity. Throughout the narrative, Saul is driven solely by self-preservation and the threat to his throne, with no demonstrated concern for the welfare of the Hebrew people. He acts out of fear and vindictiveness, attempting David's assassination and raging at his own son Jonathan for defending David. His leadership decisions are entirely self-motivated rather than oriented toward the people's wellbeing or state. There is no indication that Saul or other leaders in this passage acknowledge responsibility for how their internal power struggles and personal vendettas might affect the broader population.
